meaning:
Thugger repeats the phrase “strawberry pills,” which was censored to “Strawberry Peels” for the song’s title, to emphasize his excitement over these drugs. Drugs such as ecstasy, which Thug has dedicated an entire song to in the past, can appear in a red pressed form like the one he describes here.

Various other drugs, such as lean and weed, are mentioned throughout the song. Both can obtain a similar strawberry flavor to the one Thug describes here – marijuana can be added to a container with sliced or crushed strawberry and allow its juices to evaporate in the same environment as marijuana, which hydrates the drug along with giving it a strawberry flavor, while lean can be mixed with strawberry soda as the additive flavoring beverage.

As mentioned above, the song’s title, “Strawberry Peels,” is a censorship of this phrase, “strawberry pills,” which refers to a collection of red-colored pills. Censoring explicit words and drugs in song titles for public relations purposes is common in hip-hop, a genre that can frequently discuss more mature topics like drug use. It also recently happened to the title of Migos‘ February 2020 single “Give No Fxk,” which Thug appeared on as a featured artist.

1) The term “4-stroke” functions as a wild hyperbole for a multi-cylinder engine block. Uzi implies the girl handles sexual acts with extreme mechanical efficiency, just like an engine block orchestrates four cylinders firing at once.

2) The follow-up line, “Stand on the seat, and do tricks ho,” completely shifts the tone into a degrading, dominant command—resembling a master training a dog. Uzi orders her to get into position and perform explicit sexual acts (“do tricks”, i.e., perform oral sex) on command. By treating her skills less like a mutual encounter and more like a trained circus act or an obedience routine, Uzi asserts absolute authority and status, reducing her role to pure entertainment for the artist.

3) “She was broke, but how i kept her”: Uzi reinforces the pet dynamic by using the word “kept”. In street and financial slang, to “keep” someone means to fully support them financially. However, in this specific context, it doubles as “keeping a dog"—Uzi rescued her from poverty ("she was broke”) and now provides shelter, food, and luxury, housing her like an expensive, dependent pet.

4) “All of my niggas they kick dogs”: This final line serves as a brutal street warning and a display of zero emotional attachment. While Uzi “keeps” her, he makes it clear that his circle has no sympathy for “dogs” (promiscuous women/thots). “Kicking dogs” is a raw, violent metaphor meaning his crew treats these women with zero respect, using them and throwing them out the moment they act up or stop obeying. Yeah, bitch I smoke gas I get hella high

The second interpretation can be understood as being “high” or up, resembling fame, popularity, and stardom. Uzi exclaims that he has reached a level of success where he is beyond Earth, relative to the status of the entire planet.

Being up is a popular notion often referred to by Uzi’s close affiliate, friend, and collaborator: Young Thug. Together they have worked on tracks that include, “Yamborghini Dream”, “Dope” and “Bag”. Uzi rips the chorus as he mentions how high he gets off of Xanax, the heavily used anti-depressant used by many in the hip-hop/rap and music industry. Maxo Kream’s verses also expands on the notion of drug use mentioning other euphoric medications such as lean, percocet, codeine and adderall. This track comparably develops the idea of physically being in the sky, but only this time beyond the skies and off to another planet.

Going back to 1017 Vs. The World, the album cover illustrates four different planets, the largest one very closely resembling Mars, what scientists often call “the red planet”.
*The planet on the lower left is entire album cover shrunk.



The idea of being off the planet is a seemingly larger picture reiterated by Lil Uzi Vert throughout his entire discography.

vault_lines: Factory on my watch, make your aftermarket say, "Please tuck me"
meaning:
A factory watch is one that has stones (usually diamonds, but colored gemstones such as ruby and sapphire may also be used) which have been set into a watch piece directly by the manufacturer. Only a few factory-set gem stone watches are produced, and are usually reserved for those of high status.

In comparison, an “aftermarket” is when I luxury watch is set with gemstones by a third-party not affiliated with the luxury watch brand. Usually stones of lesser quality are used in aftermarket watches, especially when compared to the strict standards that luxury watch brands adhere too.

Take for example Rolex, who only uses high quality D through G color and Flawless to Internally Flawless diamonds in their watches. So even if an aftermarket is flooded with VVS diamonds, this would still be seen as a lesser watch as it’s quality can rarely match that of a factory set watch.

Adderall (“Addy”) is a prescription stimulant combination of amphetamine and dextroamphetamine, used recreationally to induce stimulated euphoric highs and enhance cognitive performance.

On the other hand, alcoholic substances, such as the French cognac Hennessy (“Henny”), create a more relaxed “buzzed” sense in its users.

Mixing Addy and Henny, for instance, can dull the traditional symptoms of feeling drunk or high, leading the user to take more than they otherwise would have. NAV says that when he mixes the two drugs, you best not touch him, because of the amplifying effects this has on his behavior.

Lil Uzi Vert references the Bugatti Veyron—a French supercar that once held the world record for being the fastest production car ever manufactured. The “EB” specifically refers to the Bugatti logo, which are the initials of Bugatti’s founder, Ettore Bugatti. The brand’s logo can be found subliminally stitched on the passenger and driver seats. It is worth noting that Lil Uzi Vert himself owns a Bugatti Veyron, which he purchased from the famous boxer Floyd Mayweather.

“12” is modern slang for the police, which originates from the police radio code 10-12; which alerts officers that people are present at a certain location. Referring to police as 12 is a common motif that appears throughout rap, and can be heard throughout Lil Uzi’s discography, specifically on the track “Banned from TV”. This could mean that he is trying to get away from his current location so he doesn’t have to be in a confrontation with the police.

“12” also refers to the amount of cylinders available in engines. The amount of cylinders in a car’s engine determines the rate of acceleration, and most vehicles offer a “V12” engine. In 2005, when the Veyron was first launched, the Bugatti brand made history by being the first company to offer a “W16” engine which combines two standard VR8 engines. Within his verse, Lil Uzi mistakenly refers to the car’s engine as a “V16”.

A “Choppa” originally short for “chopstick” is slang for automatic rifles such as AK-47s, Uzi’s or MAC-10’s.



Pictured: Thomson sub-machine gun

The word is referenced throughout hip-hop today and originated in the 1900s from the Thomson sub-machine gun due to the repetitive choppy sound it would make when the bullets would fire.

Uzi has previously used the term “choppa” on his 2020 hit “Celebration Station,” where he raps:

My choppa get hot just like a pan

Therefore, Lil Uzi Vert could be suggesting that although he knows his haters exist, he is so successful that he has the option to disregard their denunciation.

line: Pain
vault_lines: I'm misunderstood, she feels my pain
meaning:
In the shadowy, neon-lit labyrinth of Lil Uzi Vert’s haunted soul, pain isn’t just a word—it’s the bleeding ink used to write the dark poetry of their existence. Emerging from the digital graveyard of SoundCloud, Symere Woods took the raw, weeping wounds of emo-rock and stitched them into the heavy, thumping chest of trap music. For Uzi, pain is a beautiful nightmare, a black rose blooming in a desert of flashing cameras. By transforming their deepest heartbreaks into tragic anthems, Uzi proved that to bleed is to be alive, making pain both their ultimate curse and their most gothic muse.

To truly gaze into the abyss of Uzi’s sorrow, one must look at their darkest masterpiece, “XO Tour Llif3.” Beneath the upbeat, dancing rhythm lies a bleeding heart crying out in the dark. When Uzi screams the iconic, tear-stained refrain—"Push me to the edge / All my friends are dead"—it isn’t just lyrics; it’s a desperate plea from a soul hanging by a thread. It perfectly captures the edgy, existential agony of a broken heart numb to the world. In Uzi’s universe, you don’t heal from the trauma; you slow-dance with it in the rain, finding a twisted, beautiful euphoria in the middle of a crowded mosh pit.

But the dark clouds only grew heavier as Uzi climbed the cold mountain of fame. In albums like Luv Is Rage 2, the pain of romantic betrayal mutates into an even deeper, more hollow ache: the loneliness of a wealthy ghost. Uzi frequently weeps over how millions of dollars and designer clothes can’t buy a bandage for a broken spirit. The diamonds literally embedded into their forehead become glittering tears frozen in time—physical manifestations of a bleeding heart trying to shield itself from a cruel world. By parading their psychological scars alongside their riches, Uzi reminds us that all the gold in the world can’t fill a pitch-black void.

Ultimately, Lil Uzi Vert became the ultimate prince of darkness for a generation of broken kids. In a hip-hop culture that demanded everyone hide their tears, Uzi proudly wore their shattered heart on their sleeve like a badge of goth honor. They showed the world that it’s okay to be a beautiful mess, completely drowning in anxiety, depression, and the ruins of love. In the tragic, neon-soaked world of Lil Uzi Vert, pain is the holy water that cleanses us all—a universal ache that, when mixed with heavy bass, lets every lonely soul know they aren’t crying alone in the dark.

Because it is so crisp and smooth, it acts as a perfect chameleon in refreshing cocktails like margaritas or a simple tequila-soda, and its high-quality production typically means fewer morning-after headaches.

Hennessy, on the other hand, is a bold, rich cognac distilled from grapes and aged in French oak barrels. This process gives it a heavy, warm, and highly complex profile packed with deep notes of oak, spice, and dried fruits that demand to be sipped slowly. meaning:
Within the lyrics

I watched the moon tonight and it was red (It was red)

Lil Uzi Vert references the biblical prophecy that at the beginning of the end times the Moon will turn red. He does this to convey how his relationship has changed with his partner, the Moon’s usual “perfect” white turning to red to reflect their feelings for each other dying out, proven by the later lyrics:

But our love is not the same (Woah)
But our love is not the same

The Moon’s color change is stated in Joel 2:31, where it is prophesised that

The sun shall be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the great and awesome day of the LORD comes.

similarly in Acts 2:20 where:

the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day.

and Revelation 6:12, where:

the full moon became like blood

These all mark the beginnings of apocalyptic scenes and reflect how Uzi sees their waning love for each other; devastating and catastrophic. Additionally, the color red can be connected to blood, relating back to their dying relations bleeding out.

Uzi’s statement that

[He] wanna live together ‘til [they] dead

is him acknowledging this destructive situation that they find themselves in, wishing to live out their time together until the end, savoring it because he feels that it would be the end of his life without her, just like how he would be willing to spend his final days on Earth with this woman if the end times begun.

meaning:
Lil Peep’s unfortunate passing on November 15, 2017—caused by an overdose on Xanax and fentanyl—shocked the world. The day after the tragic news, Lil Uzi Vert knew they had to change their habits and took to twitter to announce that they would be getting sober, and that they had been struggling with shakes for the entirety of the day.

Seroquel and gabapentin are both prescription drugs that help relieve pain and shaking, prevent seizures, and balance the levels of dopamine and serotonin in the brain. These drugs could have been prescribed to Uzi to help them deal with the intense withdrawal effects that drugs like Xanax can give, including seizures, muscle spasms, and psychosis.

This line from Uzi carries several meanings. Firstly, he asks “Where you from?”, which is followed by “Throw it up”. Therefore, the question “Where you from?” can be answered appropriately with one clarifying their gang association. This could also be shown by “throwing up” a gang sign, which is mentioned right after: “Throw that shit up”.
Additionally, the phrase “Throw it up” is also a way of flexing the amount of money at one’s disposal, like “throw that money up” or “make it rain”. Uzi includes this to stick with the recurring theme throughout his music, which is that he is extremely wealthy and can have fun with his money so carelessly and without consequence that he may as well throw it up in the air.
Lastly, “Throw it up” can be interpreted in the literal sense, meaning that Uzi wants to create the imagery of himself vomiting in the listener’s head. line: Got chains on my neck like a noose, yeah
vault_lines: My shooter he all on the news, yeah, got chains on my neck like a noose, yeah
meaning:
Unsure if this was intentional, but this is actually a pretty cool critique of capitalism and touches on some themes from the society of the spectacle😭😭

At first glance, sure, the diamonds are really heavy, it looks like a noose, you choke on it, but there’s a lot of interpretation you can do.

Riches, chains and other jewelry is often portrayed as a symbol of ultimate status, a tool of liberation from the rat race. However, now that he caught the objects he chased for, he realizes that he was fed an illusion and in reality, the only thing that changed was the material for the noose that he would get symbolically executed in.

The symbolism that a noose particularly carries in the USA, being closely tied to lynchings, is hard to commercialize. It’s as if nooses got laundered to appear more fun, sparkly and glittery. It looks different enough and is way more aesthetically pleasing, which is way easier to commercialize. You turn the symbols of racial trauma from people into capital profit by selling those symbols back as toys to those people’s descendants.

It reads like a metaphor for one of the most absurd steps of turning life into a commodity, your death becoming monetized and up for public consumption. This is already referenced in the line beforehand, the fact that violence gets turned into a public product to be bought and consumed. The noose is simply the violence turned inward rather than outward, and if one is already getting sold, it is to be expected that the latter will also be sold.

The chain was never enough to be free and ultimately, he’s either consumed by the system he wanted to escape, or death is the way to escape it. Uzi never saw the liberation from capitalism that he was promised via this path of material prosperity.
